DOCUMENT_STORAGE_BUCKET_NAMEYesNoneName of the S3-compatible bucket where uploaded source files and derived page images are stored; the bucket must already exist and be in the same region as the worker fleet.
DATABASE_CONNECTION_POOL_MAX_SIZENo20Maximum number of PostgreSQL connections each API pod may hold; increase only after confirming the PgBouncer pool has sufficient headroom.

d1.purpose: Help readers configure document ingestion by finding each environment variable, its requirement, default value, and operational meaning.
tasks: Look up a variable by its exact name and read across its row.
Compare which variables are required and what defaults they use.
Read descriptions to understand behavior, dependencies, and configuration consequences.
relations: Each variable name identifies the requirement, default, and description in the same row.
Conditional requirements and operational cautions are explained in the description and must remain easy to associate with their variable.
roles: Name cells are row headers and the primary lookup anchors.
Required and Default are compact comparison columns.
Description carries the explanatory prose and needs the most flexible reading measure.
keep_whole: Environment variable names, including identifiers embedded in descriptions, should ideally remain intact.
Requirement values, numeric defaults, and the default URL should ideally remain intact.
may_wrap: Descriptions may wrap at natural word boundaries.
In a viewport-fitting layout, long identifiers and the URL may need to break within the cell.
same_scale: All row headers should use one consistent column width.
Required and Default both contain short lookup values, but Default needs more space for the URL.
Descriptions share one width even though their lengths vary.
d1.h_vs_v: Fitting the viewport avoids horizontal scrolling but forces breaks in long identifiers or the URL and produces taller rows. Scrolling can preserve lookup values and give descriptions a more comfortable measure, at the cost of hiding some columns on first sight.

d2.purpose: Document the environment variables used to configure document ingestion and related services.
tasks: Find a variable by name and check whether it is required.
Compare defaults and understand the effect and conditions of each setting.
relations: Each row binds one variable name to its requirement, default and explanatory description.
The conditional SMTP requirement depends on EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE; several descriptions also contain operational constraints.
roles: Name is the row header and primary lookup key.
Required is a compact status column; Default holds values to copy or compare.
Description carries the longer explanations and qualifications.
keep_whole: Environment variable names and references, especially when copying them.
Default values, including the URL, and the status Conditional.
Numbers and their associated units or meanings.
may_wrap: Descriptions can wrap naturally between words.
In a viewport-fitting layout, long identifiers and the URL must break because their combined minimum widths exceed the available space.
same_scale: Required and Default are both short lookup fields, although Default needs more room for the URL.
Name and Description need greater widths for different reasons: intact identifiers and readable prose.
d2.h_vs_v: Fitting the viewport puts all four fields in view but forces breaks within some identifiers and the URL. Scrolling preserves those values and gives descriptions more room, at the cost of hiding some information initially.

d3.purpose: Document the environment variables used to configure document ingestion and related services.
tasks: Find a variable by its exact name.
Check whether it is required and what value it defaults to.
Read its meaning, constraints, and operational consequences.
relations: Each row links one variable name to its requirement status, default, and explanation.
Conditional requirement for SMTP_RELAY_HOSTNAME depends on EMAIL_DELIVERY_MODE.
roles: The header identifies the four fields.
Names are row labels and lookup keys.
Required and Default are compact comparison fields.
Description supplies explanatory prose and operational qualifications.
keep_whole: The default URL, numeric values, and literal settings such as false, localhost, smtp, and ses.
may_wrap: Descriptions may wrap between words and at natural punctuation.
In a viewport-fitting layout, long identifiers and the default URL must split because their combined minimum widths exceed the available space.
same_scale: Variable names share one lookup role and should have a consistent column width.
Required and Default are compact fields, though Default needs more room for its URL.
Descriptions share the remaining prose space.
d3.h_vs_v: A fitting table keeps every field visible together but splits identifiers and creates tall rows. Scrolling preserves exact names and values; more description width reduces vertical wrapping while placing more content beyond the initial viewport.

analysis.strengths: Names, required values and defaults remain whole; descriptions have natural line breaks and at most three lines. The first viewport supports scanning names and defaults.
analysis.faults: Almost the entire description column is initially offscreen. Several descriptions occupy three lines where Q fits them into two, making the table taller.
analysis.spatial_logic: It gives the first three columns enough width for their longest values and assigns 450 px to prose, accepting horizontal scrolling to protect identifiers.

analysis.strengths: All identifiers and defaults remain whole. Its 470 px description column brings two rows down to two lines compared with P and T, making it the most compact scrolling layout shown.
analysis.faults: Descriptions are almost entirely outside the initial viewport, and reading them alongside names requires horizontal movement. The wider table increases the scroll distance slightly.
analysis.spatial_logic: It preserves the same content-sized lookup columns as P and T, then gives prose 20 px more than P; that small increase crosses useful wrapping thresholds.

analysis.strengths: The whole table is visible across the viewport, the required column stays intact, and the relatively wide name column preserves more of each identifier on its first line.
analysis.faults: Several names and the URL split within meaningful units. The narrow description column produces up to seven lines and the tallest table, with large empty areas beside the prose.
analysis.spatial_logic: It favors names over descriptions within the fixed viewport, but the extra name width is insufficient to keep the longest identifiers whole.

analysis.strengths: Everything is available without horizontal scrolling. More space for descriptions than R reduces wrapping and table height while keeping required values whole.
analysis.faults: Names break at awkward points, often within components, and the URL also splits. Descriptions still create tall rows and substantial empty space in the shorter columns.
analysis.spatial_logic: It moves 30 px from names to prose and adds 5 px to defaults compared with R, trading name continuity for more readable descriptions.

analysis.strengths: Names, required values and defaults remain intact, and descriptions wrap naturally into at most three lines.
analysis.faults: Like P and Q, almost all prose lies beyond the initial viewport. Its 10 px increase over P does not reduce any measured row height, while Q's further increase does.
analysis.spatial_logic: It uses the same protected lookup columns as P and Q, with an intermediate 460 px for descriptions.

analysis.strengths: It presents every column at once and has the shortest fitting layout. Its wider prose column gives descriptions a more comfortable measure than R or S.
analysis.faults: Several identifiers split inside components, and the default URL breaks across three lines, making it particularly difficult to read or copy visually. Some prose still occupies six lines.
analysis.spatial_logic: It minimizes the default column to give most remaining space to descriptions, accepting a severely fragmented URL and broken names.

rounds.insights: The two classes serve different tasks: scrolling preserves exact identifiers and defaults, while fitting keeps each row visible as a whole but inevitably forces some long values to break. Q is the strongest scrolling example because its extra prose width produces a useful reduction in height. U is the strongest fitting example for prose and density, though its fragmented URL is a serious lookup cost. A fitting alternative should test whether restoring the full URL is worth the narrower prose; a scrolling alternative can test whether slightly more prose width improves wrapping without excessive extra scrolling. Proposed widths are hypotheses and need rendered verification.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once, and the headers and required values fit on one line.
analysis.faults: Several variable names break inside words, and the URL breaks inside its domain. The narrow descriptions produce long, fragmented passages and very tall rows.
analysis.spatial_logic: The default column receives more room than most of its values need, while the description column is too narrow for sustained reading.

analysis.strengths: Names, default values, and words remain intact. Descriptions read naturally in two or three lines, with a compact, consistent row rhythm.
analysis.faults: At first sight almost none of the descriptions is visible; reading them requires substantial horizontal scrolling and can separate them from their row names.
analysis.spatial_logic: The first three columns use the space needed to preserve their longest entries, and the remaining wide column supports prose. Their combined width leaves the viewport boundary just inside Description.

analysis.strengths: Like s0C, it preserves names and values and keeps descriptions to at most three lines. It achieves the same row heights in 30 fewer pixels.
analysis.faults: The initial viewport still shows only a sliver of Description, and scrolling to read it weakens the connection to the names. Some prose lines are slightly more compressed than in s0C.
analysis.spatial_logic: A modest reduction in description width saves horizontal travel without changing the measured vertical rhythm; the first three columns retain their useful lookup widths.

analysis.strengths: All four columns are visible, and the wider description column gives prose a noticeably easier rhythm and shorter rows than s0B.
analysis.faults: Several variable names split within words, and the URL breaks across three lines, including inside its domain. These breaks make exact lookup and transcription harder.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space is shifted from Name and Default to Description. That improves the dominant prose but imposes a substantial cost on identifiers and the URL.

rounds.insights: The two classes make different tradeoffs. U is the stronger fitting layout for reading descriptions, but neither fitting layout preserves the long identifiers or URL. Q is the more compact scrolling layout without a measured increase in row height; both scrolling layouts preserve exact strings but initially conceal almost all prose. Further trials should test whether a small sacrifice in name or default width can reveal more description at first sight, and whether a fitting compromise can preserve the URL while retaining useful prose width.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible at once, and the required values and headers remain easy to scan.
analysis.faults: Several variable names and the URL break inside words. The narrow descriptions produce up to seven lines and make the table very tall.
analysis.spatial_logic: The wider name and default columns take space from the prose, but neither is wide enough to keep all of its content intact.

analysis.strengths: Descriptions read comfortably in two or three lines, and the URL and most names remain whole. The compact rows support comparison.
analysis.faults: Two long variable names break inside words. At first sight only a narrow portion of the description is visible, so reading it requires scrolling.
analysis.spatial_logic: This balances a useful prose measure with moderate overflow, but the saving in name-column width compromises exact identifiers.

analysis.strengths: All identifiers and the URL remain whole, descriptions are readable, and row heights are compact and consistent. The first view supports name, required-status and default lookup.
analysis.faults: The first view reveals almost none of the description, and the table requires substantial horizontal scrolling to read it.
analysis.spatial_logic: The name and default columns meet their unbroken-content thresholds, while the description receives enough width for comfortable prose. The resulting overflow is the price of preserving those units.

analysis.strengths: All columns are visible, and the broader description column makes the prose noticeably easier to read than in s1B. The table is also shorter.
analysis.faults: Several names split within words, and the URL breaks across three lines. Exact lookup and copying by eye are harder.
analysis.spatial_logic: Space shifts from names and defaults to descriptions, improving the dominant prose at the expense of identifiers.

rounds.insights: Q is the strongest scrolling layout because it preserves exact values and keeps descriptions readable, though its initial view is mainly an index. U is the stronger fitting layout for reading descriptions, while s1B gives identifiers somewhat more room but remains much taller. Within 719 px, the widths needed to keep both the longest name and URL whole leave too little space for useful descriptions, so a fitting layout must make a tradeoff.

bad.why: It breaks two environment variable names inside words despite requiring horizontal scrolling; the small width saving does not justify impairing identifier lookup.
It breaks identifiers and the URL while its narrow description column produces seven-line cells and excessive vertical separation between records.
It breaks identifiers and the URL, and its narrow description column creates tall rows that make scanning and comparison laborious.
It breaks several identifiers inside words and splits the URL; its descriptions are also more constrained than in U.

contrast.why: Equal widths fit the viewport but waste space on short required values, split many identifiers, and force descriptions into narrow, tall blocks.

synthesis.rationale: Q keeps variable names and defaults whole, gives descriptions a comfortable measure, and produces a compact, orderly table. U is the strongest fitting candidate: all four columns are visible together and descriptions have more room than in the other fitting layouts, although several identifiers and the URL break awkwardly. Q's initial viewport shows almost none of the description column, so reading explanations requires horizontal scrolling and can separate them from their names.

general: Allocate width according to content and reading task, especially the need to keep identifiers and values intact.
Judge a scrolling table both as a complete layout and through its initial viewport.
Use width where it improves meaningful line breaks and row scanning rather than imposing equal columns.
specific: The name and default columns need approximately 398 px and 190 px respectively to keep their longest values whole at the specified padding.
A description width of 470 px yields shorter rows than 450–460 px in these renders.

synthesis.tradeoffs: Q preserves identifiers and offers compact rows, but requires 438 px of horizontal scrolling and initially exposes only a sliver of the descriptions. U avoids horizontal scrolling and shows each record across the viewport, but splits identifiers and the URL and makes the table substantially taller.
synthesis.uncertain: The fitting finalist is a constrained compromise, not an unqualified recommendation: acceptance depends on how often readers must copy or distinguish exact identifiers versus read descriptions without scrolling. Actual scroll controls and their discoverability are not shown.
